text: She gave a well-known reply and turned away.
convention: Hyphenated compound 'well-known' counts as 1 word; the ASCII hyphen lives inside the token regex class so it is kept, not split.

text: "I don't know," he said, "and I don't care."
convention: Contraction 'don't' is 1 word; the apostrophe is part of the token class so it is not split. Quotation marks and commas are non-token punctuation.

text: My mother-in-law arrived before dawn, suitcase in hand.
convention: Multi-hyphen compound 'mother-in-law' is a single word; internal hyphens are kept inside one token.

text: Mr O'Brien locked the door, pocketed the key, and vanished.
convention: Name with internal apostrophe 'O'Brien' is 1 word; apostrophe is in the token class. Curly and straight apostrophes both count.

text: Rain. Wind. Silence. Then footsteps on the stair.
convention: Plain whitespace/word tokens with no edge cases; periods are non-token punctuation, so each capitalized fragment is one word.

text: The old self-made millionaire wept into his empty glass.
convention: Hyphenated compound 'self-made' counts as 1 word; hyphen kept inside the token.

text: "Run!" she screamed. He ran. The bridge groaned beneath them.
convention: Exclamation marks and quotes are non-token punctuation; every span is a plain word with no compound or numeric edge case.

text: 'Tis a long road, lad, and the season is against us.
convention: Leading-apostrophe contraction ''Tis' is treated as 1 word; the apostrophe is inside the token class so the leading mark stays attached.

text: cat — dog — bird, the labels read, each one crossed out.
convention: Em dash '—' between spaces is NOT a word and is correctly ignored (only ASCII hyphen-minus is in the token class), so the three nouns plus the rest count cleanly.

text: Hard-won, half-broken, she climbed the last ridge alone.
convention: Two hyphenated compounds 'Hard-won' and 'half-broken' each count as 1 word; hyphens kept inside their tokens.

text: He whispered her name once, twice, a third desperate time.
convention: Ordinary prose with no numeric, hyphen, or dash edge cases; straightforward whitespace word count.

text: Élodie avait déjà tout oublié quand la nuit tomba.
convention: Accented Latin letters (É, à, é) are \p{L} and stay within their tokens; nine plain words.

text: Die Straße war groß und leer; weißes Licht über allem.
convention: ß and umlauts (ß, ö, ü) are \p{L}; 'Straße', 'groß', 'weißes', 'über' each stay one token. Semicolon is non-token punctuation.

text: El niño comió rápido y corrió hacia el río pequeño.
convention: Spanish accents and ñ (í, ó, ñ) are \p{L}; ten plain words with no numeric or hyphen traps.

text: Großmutter saß am Fenster und sah dem Schnee zu, müde.
convention: ß within 'Großmutter' and 'saß', plus umlaut in 'müde', all remain inside single tokens. Ten words.

text: The blade weighed 4.5 kilos and never once dulled.
convention: A number with a decimal point ('4.5') is 1 word. The naive regex omits '.' from its token class, so it splits '4.5' into '4' and '5' and over-counts by one.

text: He counted 1,000 silent stars before the dawn broke.
convention: A comma-grouped number ('1,000') is 1 word. The naive regex omits ',' from its token class and splits it into '1' and '000', over-counting by one.

text: The reactor held at 3.14 atmospheres, then it didn't.
convention: Decimal '3.14' is 1 word (and 'didn't' is correctly 1). The naive regex splits '3.14' into '3' and '14', over-counting by one.

text: cat - dog, the chalkboard said, the dash between them stark.
convention: A lone ASCII hyphen-minus between spaces ('cat - dog') is NOT a word. The naive regex includes '-' in its token class, so the standalone dash matches as its own token and over-counts by one.

text: Wait -- stop -- listen, the radio crackled in the dark.
convention: Free-standing ASCII dash runs ('--') between spaces are not words. The naive regex matches each '--' as a token, over-counting by two.

text: Project code_name BLACKOUT was never meant to leak.
convention: An underscore-joined compound ('code_name') reads as a single word under the compound = 1 rule. The naive regex excludes '_' from its token class and splits it into 'code' and 'name', over-counting by one.

text: The train left at 3:30 and would not wait for stragglers.
convention: A clock time ('3:30') is a single numeric word. The naive regex omits ':' and splits it into '3' and '30', over-counting by one.

text: Sales jumped 50.5% in a single feverish afternoon.
convention: A decimal percentage ('50.5%') is one numeric word. The naive regex drops '%' (fine) but also splits on the '.', yielding '50' and '5', over-counting by one.

text: Le thermomètre indiquait 37,5 degrés sous la lune.
convention: French decimals use a comma ('37,5'), which is still 1 word. The naive regex splits on ',' into '37' and '5', over-counting by one.

text: La factura sumaba 2.500 pesos, dijo el tendero, ceñudo.
convention: Spanish uses '.' as a thousands separator ('2.500' = two thousand five hundred), one numeric word. The naive regex splits on '.' into '2' and '500', over-counting by one.
